subtopic_detail: post exercise facilitation and autonomic features distinguishing a presynaptic neuromuscular disorder from myasthenia
stem:
You are the neurology registrar assessing a 63 year old man referred with four months of difficulty getting out of a low chair and climbing the stairs at home. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily since he was twenty three.

He volunteers that his mouth has been persistently dry, that he has become constipated and that he has had difficulty with erections over the same period. He denies double vision and says his eyelids do not droop as the day goes on. On testing, his knee reflexes are absent, but after he holds a sustained quadriceps contraction for fifteen seconds they become obtainable, and his grip feels briefly stronger after repeated effort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 128/80 lying with a 14 mmHg systolic fall on standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal lower limb weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes at rest which return after sustained contraction, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, dry oral mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, chest radiograph reported as no focal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies with repetitive nerve stimulation
options.rationale: This pairing targets the postsynaptic disorder, in which fatigable ptosis and diplopia dominate, reflexes are preserved and strength worsens rather than improves with repeated effort. The two conditions are distinguished by the direction of the response to exercise, and here strength and reflexes both improve. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with a lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands
options.rationale: Oligoclonal bands support a central demyelinating process, which would give upper motor neuron signs rather than absent reflexes. Nerve conduction studies alone, without repetitive stimulation protocols, will not capture the presynaptic abnormality. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: A cord or cauda equina lesion could produce lower limb weakness with areflexia and bladder or bowel disturbance, which gives this option some surface plausibility. It would not produce dry mouth, would not improve with sustained contraction and would be expected to give sensory and sphincter findings that he does not have. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Creatine kinase with electromyography and a subsequent muscle biopsy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy is a standard differential for subacute proximal weakness, but the creatine kinase is already within normal limits and a primary muscle disease does not explain the autonomic symptoms or the facilitation. Biopsy would subject him to a procedure that does not address the discriminating findings. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Chest computed tomography with voltage gated calcium channel antibodies
options.rationale: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post exercise facilitation of reflexes indicates a presynaptic defect of acetylcholine release, which in a heavy smoker of this age is paraneoplastic in around half of cases and most often driven by a small cell lung carcinoma. The tumour frequently precedes the neurological presentation and a plain radiograph is insufficiently sensitive to exclude it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

explanation.summary: Presynaptic failure of acetylcholine release produces a triad of proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction and reduced or absent tendon reflexes, and the reflexes characteristically return after ten to fifteen seconds of sustained voluntary contraction because repeated activity increases calcium entry at the nerve terminal. This post exercise facilitation is the bedside finding that separates it from the postsynaptic disorder, where sustained effort worsens weakness. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic and the tumour is almost always small cell lung carcinoma, with the neurological syndrome preceding the cancer by months to years, so a normal chest radiograph does not close the question and computed tomography is required, with consideration of positron emission tomography and repeated surveillance over two years if the initial imaging is clear. Antibodies to the P and Q type voltage gated calcium channel are found in most patients and confirm the diagnosis. Treatment of the tumour often improves the neurology, with amifampridine used symptomatically alongside immunotherapy for the non paraneoplastic form.
key_points: Proximal weakness plus autonomic features plus areflexia is the presynaptic triad
Post exercise facilitation of reflexes is the discriminating bedside sign
Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung carcinoma
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude the tumour and computed tomography is required
Voltage gated calcium channel antibodies confirm the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Test for post exercise facilitation by eliciting an absent reflex, having the patient sustain a maximal contraction of that muscle group for ten to fifteen seconds, then immediately re-testing; return of the reflex points to a presynaptic disorder and should trigger chest imaging for small cell lung cancer.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: screening for the diabetes of cystic fibrosis when the glycated haemoglobin is within normal limits
stem:
You are the registrar in the adult cystic fibrosis clinic reviewing a 24 year old woman at her routine appointment. Her forced expiratory volume in one second is 62 per cent predicted and she has been established on modulator therapy for two years.

She has lost 4 kg over the past four months. She takes her pancreatic enzyme replacement with every meal and snack and her dietitian confirms her adherence and her intake have not changed. She has needed two courses of intravenous antibiotics for exacerbations in the past six months, up from none in the preceding year. She has noticed she is thirstier than usual but has not changed her diet.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19.1 kg/m2 down from 20.6 kg/m2 four months ago, scattered coarse crackles bilaterally, no clubbing change
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 5.9 per cent (less than 6.0), random plasma glucose 8.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), faecal elastase low consistent with known pancreatic insufficiency, liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Two hour 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test arranged in the next week
options.rationale: The oral glucose tolerance test is the standard annual screen from adolescence in this population and is the appropriate test now, because the characteristic early abnormality is postprandial hyperglycaemia with a preserved fasting glucose. Unexplained weight loss and a rising exacerbation frequency are the classic prompts to test outside the annual schedule. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia)

options.text: Repeat the glycated haemoglobin in three months and review the weight
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in this population because shortened red cell survival from chronic inflammation and recurrent infection falsely lowers the result, so a value within normal limits does not exclude the diagnosis. Repeating an insensitive test after a further three months of weight loss compounds the delay. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia)

options.text: Fasting plasma glucose on two separate mornings in the coming fortnight
options.rationale: The fasting glucose remains within normal limits until relatively late in this condition because residual insulin secretion covers the basal state while failing to cover meals. Relying on it misses the window in which treatment protects lung function and weight. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

options.text: Two weeks of continuous glucose monitoring with a clinic review after
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring detects postprandial excursions sensitively and is increasingly used in this group, which makes it a genuine near miss. It has not replaced the glucose tolerance test as the diagnostic standard, and the diagnostic thresholds that direct insulin therapy are defined against the tolerance test. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

options.text: Random plasma glucose with urinary ketones at the next clinic review
options.rationale: A random glucose lacks the sensitivity to establish the diagnosis and ketosis is characteristically absent in this form of diabetes because insulin deficiency is partial rather than complete. A negative result would provide false reassurance. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis related diabetes arises from progressive destruction of the pancreatic islets by the same fibrotic process that causes exocrine insufficiency, and it affects a substantial proportion of adults with the condition, with prevalence rising steeply with age. It sits apart from both type 1 and type 2 diabetes: insulin deficiency is partial so ketoacidosis is rare, insulin resistance fluctuates with infection and corticosteroid use, and the earliest abnormality is postprandial rather than fasting hyperglycaemia. Its clinical importance is that unexplained weight loss, a decline in lung function and increasing exacerbation frequency precede the diagnosis by up to several years, and these outcomes improve with insulin therapy, which is the treatment of choice rather than oral agents. Annual screening with an oral glucose tolerance test from about ten years of age is standard, with additional testing whenever there is unexplained decline. Glycated haemoglobin is specifically not recommended as the screening test because red cell turnover in this population makes it falsely reassuring.
key_points: Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in cystic fibrosis because of shortened red cell survival
The oral glucose tolerance test is the annual screen and the diagnostic standard
Postprandial hyperglycaemia precedes any fasting abnormality
Unexplained weight loss, falling lung function and more frequent exacerbations are the clinical prompts
Insulin, not an oral agent, is the treatment of choice
explanation.pearls: In cystic fibrosis related diabetes the decline in weight and forced expiratory volume in one second begins two to four years before the glucose tolerance test becomes diagnostic, so an unexplained fall in either is itself the indication to test regardless of the annual schedule.

subtopic_detail: new mononeuritis multiplex with marked eosinophilia in a patient carrying an asthma label
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44 year old man in the emergency department. He has carried a diagnosis of asthma for six years, takes a high dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long acting beta agonist, and has had nasal polyps removed twice.

Three weeks ago he developed a right foot drop that has not improved, and over the past week the ring and little fingers of his left hand have become numb and weak. He has a non blanching purple rash over both shins. He has not travelled overseas and has not started any new medication in the past year. His bloods and chest film are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right foot drop with weak ankle dorsiflexion, sensory loss in the left ulnar distribution with weak finger abduction, palpable purpura over both shins, expiratory wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 4.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 66 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine within normal limits, urinalysis within normal limits, troponin mildly raised
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral migratory infiltrates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate the inhaled therapy and add a monoclonal anti interleukin 5 agent
options.rationale: Treating this as refractory eosinophilic asthma addresses the wheeze while leaving a vasculitis to infarct further nerves and myocardium. Biologic therapy targeting interleukin 5 does have a role in this condition, but as a steroid sparing agent after remission is induced, not as the acute response to progressive nerve and cardiac involvement. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Commence high dose oral corticosteroid today with urgent specialist referral
options.rationale: Late onset asthma with nasal polyps, marked eosinophilia, palpable purpura and mononeuritis multiplex constitutes an eosinophilic small vessel vasculitis with active neurological and probable cardiac involvement, which is an indication for immediate corticosteroid while specialist assessment and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing proceed. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death in this condition and drives the urgency. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies and review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies will confirm the pattern of multiple separate named nerve lesions and are worth obtaining, but the tempo is wrong. Each week of untreated disease risks a further infarcted nerve with incomplete recovery, and the raised troponin signals organ involvement that will not wait. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Send strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin before any steroid
options.rationale: Excluding strongyloides before immunosuppression is genuinely important because hyperinfection can be fatal, and serology should be sent today, but it is drawn in parallel rather than used to delay treatment. He has no overseas travel or endemic residence, and the neurological progression will not pause for a serology result. (Source: Australian Society for Infectious Diseases)

options.text: Refer for skin prick allergy testing and commence a leukotriene antagonist
options.rationale: Allergy testing addresses the atopic label he has carried rather than the vasculitic process now causing his deficits. Leukotriene antagonists have historically been associated with unmasking this condition when corticosteroid is reduced, and they have no therapeutic role in the acute vasculitis. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis evolves through three overlapping phases: an allergic phase with adult onset asthma and sinonasal disease, an eosinophilic phase with peripheral eosinophilia and tissue infiltration producing migratory pulmonary infiltrates or eosinophilic gastroenteritis, and a vasculitic phase with neuropathy, purpura, cardiac and renal involvement. The asthma label typically precedes the vasculitis by several years, which is why the condition is so often first recognised at the moment a patient labelled asthmatic develops a neurological deficit. Mononeuritis multiplex, meaning deficits in two or more separately named peripheral nerves, is the classic neurological signature and occurs in the majority. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in only about forty per cent and a negative result therefore cannot exclude the diagnosis, which is a frequent source of delay. Cardiac involvement, which may present with only a raised troponin, is the principal cause of mortality and shifts treatment toward combined corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
key_points: Adult onset asthma with nasal polyps plus eosinophilia plus neuropathy is the defining combination
Mononeuritis multiplex means deficits in two or more separately named nerves
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in only about forty per cent
Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death and may show only as a raised troponin
Send strongyloides serology in parallel with, not instead of, starting corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: A peripheral eosinophil count above 1.5 x10^9/L in someone carrying an asthma label who develops a new foot drop should prompt same day corticosteroid and vasculitis referral, because an infarcted nerve left untreated beyond a few weeks recovers poorly.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy
Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists
